{{Short description|Mathematics concept}}
{{Orphan|date=May 2025}}

In mathematics, and especially [[topology]], a '''Pytkeev space''' is a [[topological space]] that satisfies qualities more subtle than a [[Convergent series|convergence]] of a [[sequence]]. They are named after E. G. Pytkeev, who proved in 1983 that [[sequential space]]s have this property.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Pytkeev | first = E. G.
 | journal = Trudy Matematicheskogo Instituta imeni V. A. Steklova
 | mr = 733840
 | pages = 209–213
 | title = Maximally decomposable spaces
 | volume = 154
 | year = 1983}}.</ref>

== Definitions ==

Let ''X'' be a topological space. For a subset ''S'' of ''X'' let <span style="text-decoration: overline;">''S''</span> denote the [[closure (topology)|closure]] of ''S''. Then a point ''x'' is called a ''Pytkeev point'' if for every set A with {{nowrap|1=''x'' ∈ <span style="text-decoration: overline;">''A'' \ {''x''}</span>}}, there is a countable <math> \pi </math>-net of infinite subsets of ''A''. A ''Pytkeev space'' is a space in which every point is a Pytkeev point.<ref name="TAIA">{{cite journal|last1=Malykhin|first1=V. I.|last2=Tironi|first2=G|year=2000|title=Weakly Fréchet–Urysohn and Pytkeev spaces|journal=Topology and Its Applications|volume=104|issue=2|pages=181–190|doi=10.1016/s0166-8641(99)00027-9|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Examples==

* Every [[sequential space]] is also a Pytkeev space. This is because, if {{nowrap|1=''x'' ∈ <span style="text-decoration: overline;">''A'' \ {''x''}</span>}} then there exists a sequence {''a<sub>k</sub>''} that converges to ''x''. So take the countable π-net of infinite subsets of ''A'' to be {{nowrap|1={''A<sub>k</sub>''} = {''a<sub>k</sub>'', ''a''<sub>''k''+1</sub>, ''a''<sub>''k''+2</sub>, …}}}.<ref name="TAIA"/>
* If ''X'' is a Pytkeev space, then it is also a [[Weakly Fréchet–Urysohn space]].
